questions.question: How do you integrate the OpenAI API into a Spring Boot application using Spring AI?
questions.title: OpenAI API Integration in Spring Boot with Spring AI
questions.direct_answer: Add the `spring-ai-openai-spring-boot-starter` dependency, set `spring.ai.openai.api-key` in `application.properties`, and inject `ChatClient` or `OpenAiChatModel`. Call `chatClient.prompt().user("your prompt").call().content()` to get a response. Spring AI handles HTTP, retries, and model configuration through auto-configuration.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows Spring AI's auto-configuration approach, how API keys flow through properties, and the ChatClient fluent API
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Manually wiring HTTP clients when Spring AI's auto-configuration handles it; not using the ChatClient builder pattern and going straight to the lower-level model
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention model-level options like temperature and max tokens via ChatOptions, streaming responses via stream().content(), and how to swap providers by changing the starter dependency

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- `spring.ai.openai.api-key` is the only required property.
- `ChatClient` is the high-level fluent API; `OpenAiChatModel` is the lower-level model bean.
- Streaming uses `.stream().content()` which returns a `Flux<String>`.
- Swap providers by swapping the starter — `ChatClient` code stays the same.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
All three are supported by Spring AI starters: `spring-ai-openai`, `spring-ai-anthropic`, `spring-ai-vertex-ai-gemini`.

The `ChatClient` interface is identical across providers — swap the starter and properties to switch.

Key differences: OpenAI uses `OpenAiChatModel`, Anthropic uses `AnthropicChatModel`, Google uses `VertexAiGeminiChatModel`. Auth differs — OpenAI and Anthropic use API keys, Gemini on Vertex AI uses service account credentials. Token context windows and pricing vary significantly.

Manually wiring HTTP clients when Spring AI's auto-configuration handles it; not using the ChatClient builder pattern and going straight to the lower-level model

seo.metaTitle: OpenAI API Spring Boot Integration with Spring AI — ChatClient Setup
seo.metaDescription: Step-by-step guide to integrating OpenAI API into a Spring Boot app with Spring AI: dependencies, API key config, ChatClient usage, and streaming responses.

familiarity_anchors: Spring Boot starter + application.properties for API key
ChatClient is the fluent call API Spring AI exposes
OpenAiChatModel is the lower-level bean if you need direct access
speakable_v2.hook: Spring AI's trick is that you don't write any HTTP code. You add a starter, drop in an API key, and it's wired. Here's what that looks like.

beats.text: Spring AI is an abstraction layer over LLM vendor APIs. It auto-configures an `OpenAiChatModel` bean and a `ChatClient` builder when it sees the right starter on the classpath. You interact with the model through `ChatClient`, never touching raw HTTP.

Before Spring AI, you'd either use the vendor's Java SDK directly or roll your own `RestTemplate` / `WebClient` setup — with separate retry, serialization, and config logic for each provider. Spring AI gives you one consistent interface, so switching from OpenAI to Anthropic doesn't rewrite your service.

groups.heading: The starter
groups.text: The spring-ai-openai-spring-boot-starter pulls in the SDK and registers the auto-configuration class. One dependency starts the whole chain.

groups.heading: The API key
groups.text: Set spring.ai.openai.api-key in application.properties pointing to an env var. Never hardcode it — that's a sharp edge that ends up in git history.

groups.heading: ChatClient
groups.text: The fluent entry point. Inject the builder, call build once, then use prompt, user, call, content per request.

groups.heading: OpenAiChatModel
groups.text: The lower-level bean. It's available when you need per-request options, but ChatClient covers most use cases.

paragraphs: Three config lines connect you: the starter in pom.xml, the api-key property pointing at an env var, and optionally the model name like gpt-4o.
Then you inject ChatClient.Builder, build the client once in the constructor, and call prompt, user, call, content per request to get the model's text back.

items: Hardcoding the API key instead of referencing an env var — keys end up in git history and it's a non-obvious leak.
Injecting OpenAiChatModel directly when ChatClient makes switching providers much easier later.
Ignoring token limits — long prompts silently truncate or throw an error depending on the model.
Not setting a timeout — the default HTTP client timeout may be much longer than your SLA allows.

speakable_v2.cap: Add the starter, point the api-key property at an env var, inject ChatClient.Builder, and you're making calls. The abstraction pays off when you swap providers.
followup_handoff: How do you stream tokens back to the browser instead of waiting for the full response?
How do you pass a system prompt and control temperature per individual request?
What changes if you swap to the Anthropic starter instead of OpenAI?

questions.question: How do you handle LLM API rate limits and implement retry logic in a Spring Boot service?
questions.title: Handling LLM API Rate Limits and Retry Logic in Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: Use Spring Retry's `@Retryable` with exponential backoff for transient `429` errors. Layer Resilience4j circuit breaker on top to stop hammering the API when rate limits are sustained. For token-based limits, use a token bucket (e.g., Guava `RateLimiter`) before sending requests. Always log retry attempts and propagate a meaningful error to callers when the circuit opens.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate distinguishes per-minute rate limits from token-per-minute limits, knows the tools (Spring Retry, Resilience4j), and can articulate when to stop retrying
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Retrying immediately on a 429 — it makes the problem worse. Not distinguishing RPM (requests per minute) from TPM (tokens per minute). Opening the circuit breaker too aggressively on a cold start.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention request-level token counting before sending (estimate prompt tokens), tracking remaining quota from response headers, and degrading gracefully to a cached response or a simpler prompt

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Spring Retry** handles transient 429s — exponential backoff with jitter is the right shape.
- **Resilience4j** prevents cascading failure when the API is consistently overloaded.
- **Token bucket** (Guava `RateLimiter`) client-side limits prevents hitting the API limit in the first place.
- Check `x-ratelimit-remaining-tokens` response headers to adapt before hitting the limit.

sections.title: Option 1 — Exponential Backoff with Spring Retry
Option 2 — Circuit Breaker with Resilience4j
sections.content:
```java
@CircuitBreaker(name = "llm-api", fallbackMethod = "cachedFallback")
public String call(String prompt) {
    return chatClient.prompt().user(prompt).call().content();
}
```

Configure in `application.yml`:
```yaml
resilience4j:
  circuitbreaker:
    instances:
      llm-api:
        slidingWindowSize: 10
        failureRateThreshold: 50
        waitDurationInOpenState: 30s
```

seo.metaTitle: LLM API Rate Limits in Spring Boot — Retry, Circuit Breaker, Token Bucket
seo.metaDescription: Handle OpenAI rate limits in Spring Boot: exponential backoff with Spring Retry, circuit breaker with Resilience4j, token bucket with Guava RateLimiter, and graceful degradation.

familiarity_anchors: LLM APIs return HTTP 429 when you send too many requests per minute
Spring Retry's @Retryable handles transient failures with backoff
Resilience4j circuit breaker stops retrying when a service is consistently down
speakable_v2.standard_example: @Retryable with exponential backoff on 429 + @CircuitBreaker fallback when the quota is sustained
speakable_v2.hook: A 429 from OpenAI doesn't mean your code is broken. It means you're sending requests faster than your quota allows. The question is how to slow down without crashing your service.

beats.text: Cost and reliability pull in opposite directions. Retrying on a sustained rate limit burns quota without helping. But a raw 429 surfaced to the caller is a poor user experience when a brief pause would've gotten through.

groups.heading: Exponential backoff
groups.text: Spring Retry's @Retryable with @Backoff, doubling the wait up to 4 tries. Good for short-lived spikes.

groups.heading: Circuit breaker
groups.text: Resilience4j @CircuitBreaker stops calling the API entirely after a failure threshold. Good for sustained limits.

groups.heading: Token bucket
groups.text: Guava RateLimiter client-side. Proactively limits your send rate so you never hit the API limit in the first place.

beats.text: Layer them. RateLimiter first, @Retryable for bursts that slip through, @CircuitBreaker as the outer net. Check remaining-tokens response headers and slow down dynamically before hitting the limit.

items: When every call hits rate limits, upgrade the plan or shorten prompts — more retries won't fix a quota problem.
If the circuit breaker trips constantly, your timeout's likely too short for the model's latency.

speakable_v2.cap: Layer token bucket first, then exponential backoff, then a circuit breaker. Each catches what the previous misses. If you're retrying every call, the quota tier is the real problem.
followup_handoff: When should the circuit breaker open on latency spikes, not just error rates?
How do you estimate prompt token count before sending to stay within TPM limits?
What's the right fallback when the circuit is open — cached response, simpler model, or hard error?

questions.question: What is function calling in LLM APIs and how do you implement it with Spring AI?
questions.title: LLM Function Calling with Spring AI — FunctionCallback and @Bean Registration
questions.direct_answer: Function calling lets the LLM decide to invoke a registered Java function instead of returning plain text. The model returns a JSON payload with the function name and arguments; your code executes it and sends the result back. In Spring AI, register functions as `FunctionCallback` beans and pass them via `FunctionCallingOptions`. Spring AI handles the round-trip automatically.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the two-phase request cycle (initial call + tool-result call), knows how to register functions in Spring AI, and can explain when function calling is better than prompt engineering
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking function calling executes server-side code directly — the model just returns a JSON intent; your code does the actual execution. Registering functions with wrong parameter types so the model can't serialize arguments.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss parallel tool calls (multiple functions invoked in one turn), function call streaming, and how to validate and sanitize the model's returned arguments before executing them

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- `FunctionCallback` wraps your Java function with a name, description, and input schema.
- `FunctionCallingOptions` tells the model which functions are available for this request.
- The model decides whether to call a function — you don't control that choice.
- Spring AI handles the second request (sending tool results back) automatically.
- Always validate and sanitize the model's returned arguments before executing them.

seo.metaTitle: LLM Function Calling in Spring AI — FunctionCallback Setup and Registration
seo.metaDescription: Implement function calling with Spring AI: register Java functions as FunctionCallback beans, pass FunctionCallingOptions, and handle the model's tool-call round-trip automatically.

familiarity_anchors: The LLM doesn't execute your code — it returns a JSON intent describing which function to call
Spring AI's FunctionCallback wraps a Java method with a name and schema the model can understand
FunctionCallingOptions attaches available functions to a specific ChatClient request
speakable_v2.standard_example: FunctionCallback wrapping a weather lookup — model asks for city weather, your service fetches it, model uses the result in its answer
speakable_v2.hook: Function calling sounds like the model runs your code. It doesn't. It tells you what to run. That distinction matters for security and design. Here's how Spring AI wires it up.

beats.text: Function calling is a protocol where the model, instead of answering directly, returns a structured JSON message saying which function it wants called and with what arguments. Your code runs the function, sends the result back, and the model finishes its answer. Spring AI calls these functions FunctionCallback objects.

LLMs don't have live data. Function calling lets the model request it without stuffing everything into the prompt context. It's cleaner, cheaper in tokens, and lets the model decide when fresh data is needed.

groups.heading: FunctionCallback
groups.text: Wraps a Java function with a name, a description (used by the model to decide when to call it), and an input record type that Spring AI serializes into a JSON schema.

groups.heading: FunctionCallingOptions
groups.text: Tells the model which functions are available in a given request. Expose only what's needed per request — not every call should have access to everything.

groups.heading: The round-trip
groups.text: Request 1: model sees the prompt and function definitions. Model returns a tool-call JSON. Spring AI detects it, calls your function, sends the result back as Request 2. Model returns the final text.

paragraphs: Register the function as a @Bean using FunctionCallback.builder, giving it the name getCurrentWeather, a lambda calling your WeatherService, a description, and an inputType pointing to a Java record with a city field.
In the ChatClient call, attach FunctionCallingOptions with that function name via the options method. Spring AI handles both request legs automatically and returns the model's final text.

items: Assuming the model always calls your function — it decides. A vague description is a hidden risk.
Skipping validation of the model's returned arguments — treat them like untrusted user input.
Exposing all functions on all requests — scope them to what each call actually needs.

speakable_v2.cap: The model returns intent, your code acts on it. Register FunctionCallback beans, pass them via FunctionCallingOptions, and validate arguments before executing.

Auth differs — OpenAI and Anthropic use API keys, Gemini on Vertex AI uses service account credentials. Token context windows and pricing vary significantly.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands that Spring AI abstracts the vendor differences, knows the auth model for each, and can articulate when to pick one over another
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking you need separate client code for each provider — Spring AI's ChatClient abstraction means the service layer doesn't change when you switch. Forgetting that Vertex AI uses GCP IAM instead of a simple API key.

sections.title: When to Pick Each
sections.content:
- **OpenAI**: Best ecosystem, most function calling examples, widest community support.
- **Anthropic**: Strong for long-document analysis and instruction following; 200K context window.
- **Gemini**: Best for multi-modal (text + image + video), 1M token context, natively on GCP.
- **All three**: Same `ChatClient` API in Spring AI — switching costs only a properties change.

seo.metaTitle: OpenAI vs Anthropic vs Google Gemini — Java Spring AI Integration Comparison
seo.metaDescription: Compare OpenAI, Anthropic Claude, and Google Gemini from a Java backend perspective: Spring AI starters, auth models, context windows, function calling, and when to pick each.

familiarity_anchors: Spring AI exposes the same ChatClient regardless of which provider is wired in
OpenAI and Anthropic use API keys; Vertex AI uses GCP service account credentials
Context window sizes differ — Gemini 1.5 Pro supports up to 1 million tokens
speakable_v2.standard_example: Swap spring-ai-openai-spring-boot-starter for spring-ai-anthropic-spring-boot-starter — the ChatClient call in your service doesn't change
speakable_v2.hook: Three major LLM providers, one Spring AI abstraction. The ChatClient code doesn't change when you switch providers. What does change is auth, context window, and pricing — here's what to know.

groups.heading: OpenAI
groups.text: Starter: spring-ai-openai. Bean: OpenAiChatModel. Auth: API key. GPT-4o has 128K context. It's the widest ecosystem.

groups.heading: Anthropic Claude
groups.text: Starter: spring-ai-anthropic. Bean: AnthropicChatModel. Auth: API key. Claude 3.5 has 200K context. It's strong on long docs.

groups.heading: Google Gemini
groups.text: Starter: spring-ai-vertex-ai-gemini. Bean: VertexAiGeminiChatModel. Auth: GCP service account, not an API key. Gemini 1.5 Pro has 1M context and it's multi-modal.

paragraphs: Pick OpenAI when you want the richest ecosystem. It's the default for most new projects.
Pick Anthropic when you've got large documents or complex instructions — the 200K window and Claude's instruction following are strong there.
Pick Gemini when you're already on GCP or need multi-modal input at scale. The 1M context is genuinely useful for huge codebases or long documents.
The service code's identical for all three. Only the starter and properties change. OpenAiChatModel, AnthropicChatModel, and VertexAiGeminiChatModel all satisfy the same ChatModel interface.

The gotcha candidates miss: Vertex AI doesn't use a simple API key. It needs a GCP service account or Application Default Credentials — that's a non-trivial auth setup that surprises teams moving from OpenAI.

speakable_v2.cap: Spring AI's abstraction means switching providers is a properties change, not a refactor. The real tradeoffs are auth complexity, context window size, and which cloud you're already on.
